topic.title: Cooperation & Listening
topic.description: Build cooperation so you don't have to repeat yourself or shout

articles.title: When "Not Listening" Isn't the Problem
articles.description: "Not listening" is almost always a mislabel.
articles.content:
# When "Not Listening" Isn't the Problem

"Not listening" is almost always a mislabel. A child who ignores a request they don't want to do isn't failing to hear you — they're declining to cooperate, and those are different problems with different fixes. Trying to make them "hear better" aims at the wrong target. The shift that changes everything is small: stop lining up against your child, and start lining up with them against the thing that's hard.

## Why This Works

Think of the last time your child "didn't listen." Now picture offering them something they love — they hear that instantly. Hearing was never the issue; wanting was. Call it a listening problem and you go hunting for volume and repetition, and you pin the whole failure on the child. Rename it "we're having trouble cooperating" and two things move at once: the problem becomes something between you rather than a flaw inside them, and you stop reaching for the tools that don't work (louder, again, sharper) and start reaching for the ones that do. A quick test on yourself: you're deep in an email when your partner calls over, wanting the dinner decision right now. "Not now," you say. Nobody would call that a listening problem. The refusal was never about your ears — it was timing, absorption, and being asked for something you didn't want right then. The same forces are at work with your child. And a flat "no," loudest around age three and again in the teen years, is often a child trying on a self, not aiming a weapon at you.

## What To Do

- Catch yourself before "why won't you listen?" and swap the question in your head: "why is cooperating hard right now?"
- Picture it as you-and-your-child on one side and the hard moment on the other — not you versus them.
- If you're too heated to find that stance, step back and steady yourself first; you can't lead from an enemy posture.
- Keep your authority. Being on your child's side doesn't dissolve the limit — you still decide, you just stop treating them as the opponent.
- When only bad options come to mind ("give in or drag them out"), treat that as a sign the question is framed wrong, not that you must pick one.

## What To Say

- "Looks like this one's tough to get moving on. Let's figure it out together."
- To yourself: "Not an ears problem. A cooperation problem. Different fix."
- "I'm not going to fight you on this — and it's still happening. We'll find the how together."

## Common Pitfalls

- Turning up the volume and the repetitions, as if the message didn't land — it landed; the willingness didn't.
- Reading an ordinary "no" as disrespect and meeting it like an attack.
- Dropping all authority in the name of teamwork — being on their side isn't the same as having no line.
- Making it a character verdict ("she never listens") instead of a moment to solve.

## When To Seek Support

If a child past the toddler years shows almost no give-and-take cooperation anywhere — home, care settings, with other kids — or genuinely doesn't seem to process spoken language, that's worth a conversation with your pediatrician to rule out a hearing or language piece. See the red-flags card.

articles.content:
# What's Underneath the Resistance

When cooperation is hard, it's usually one of three things: a young brain wired for right-now over later, an instruction with too many steps crammed in, or a tank of independence run low after a whole day of being told what to do. None of these is defiance. Each has a different, doable fix — and the strength of your everyday connection shifts a given moment more than the wording of any single request.

## Why This Works

A young brain chases the reward it can feel now and discounts the one that's far off or belongs to your schedule — that's normal wiring, not selfishness. It's why "come get a berry" works instantly while "shoes on so we're not late" doesn't: one payoff is here, the other is yours and later. Multi-step asks land differently too. "Get dressed, brush teeth, and grab your bag" can flood a small working memory, and what pours out looks like refusal but is really overwhelm. And every child spends the day being steered — do this, stop that, hurry — and like any of us, the more they're directed, the more they need a little say back. That need doesn't evaporate; it surfaces at the next small ask, which is how a tiny request draws a giant "no." Under all of it sits one quiet truth: how connected your child feels to you in general moves the odds of any single moment more than the perfect phrase does. A warmed-up relationship forgives a clumsy request; a depleted one refuses a polished one.

## What To Do

- Match the fix to the cause. For a right-now brain, put something good on this side of the task: "shoes first, then you pick the walk-song." Not a bribe — just a nearer reason.
- Cut compound instructions to one step. Say the next thing, not the whole list.
- Before an ask that pulls them out of their world, spend ten seconds in it first — notice what they're building, join it a beat — so the request has something to cross on.
- Spend your good moments on purpose: a hard request costs a little goodwill, and unhurried warmth earlier in the day is what refills it. If refusals are constant, add warmth before you re-word.
- When you must say no to one thing, hand back a real choice on another — which cup, which order, which route — so the hunger for some control gets fed somewhere.

## What To Say

- "First shoes, then you're the boss of the music. Deal?"
- "Just the socks for now. The rest comes after."
- "Whoa — look at that tower. Tell me the plan… okay, and in two minutes it's cleanup."
- "You don't get to skip the bath. You do get to pick: before the story or after?"

## Common Pitfalls

- Hearing overwhelm as defiance and answering a too-long list with a louder version of the same too-long list.
- Reasoning about a far-off payoff to a brain that only feels the near one.
- Re-wording the same request ten ways when the real shortfall is connection, not clarity.
- Offering a "choice" over the non-negotiable itself ("do you want to brush teeth?") instead of over how or when it happens.

## When To Seek Support

If a child consistently can't follow even single, simple steps that same-age kids manage, or words seem not to register at all, mention it to your pediatrician to rule out attention, processing, or hearing factors. See the red-flags card.

articles.title: Building Cooperation Before You Need It
articles.description: The most powerful listening work happens when nothing's being asked.
articles.content:
# Building Cooperation Before You Need It

The most powerful listening work happens when nothing's being asked. Small, low-stakes deposits — practicing waiting, playing with "no," rehearsing a hard moment before it's live, choosing not to react — build a child who can cooperate when it counts. This chapter leans on what the defiance guides already cover for protected one-on-one time and letting your child take charge, and adds the pieces specific to listening.

## Why This Works

Skills you want in a hard moment have to be built in easy ones — a child can't first practice waiting, or handling a "no," at the exact second it's hardest. So you rehearse in peacetime. Slipping a small, named wait between what your child wants and when they get it — even when you could hand it over instantly — slowly grows the muscle for tolerating "not yet." Letting them fire off silly, pretend refusals at a calm moment drains some of the charge out of the real ones. And quietly choosing not to react to low-grade resistance — not as giving up, but as a decision — often lets it burn out on its own instead of your reaction feeding it more oxygen. (This is only for safe moments; if anyone's in danger, that's the next chapter, and you act.) Underneath all of it is the read you carry: a child you've privately decided is "giving you a hard time" gets a colder version of you, and cold doesn't earn cooperation. Reaching for the kindest believable explanation of their behavior restores your own warmth first — and warmth is what the child actually answers.

## What To Do

- Practice waiting on purpose. When your child wants something you could give right away, sometimes add a short, narrated pause: "You want it now — waiting's hard — let's count to ten, then it's yours."
- Play with refusal when nothing's at stake: take turns lobbing goofy, over-the-top "no way!"s at each other, so "no" becomes something you share, not only something you fight over.
- Rehearse the hard thing early — walk a tricky transition in slow motion as a game, or say the calm line you'll need out loud to yourself before the moment, so it's loaded when you reach for it.
- When resistance is minor and safe, do less — pause, stay near, and let it pass instead of jumping in to fix or correct.
- Before you respond to a "won't," reach for the most generous believable reason — tired, thrown by a change, not finished with the last thing — and say it in your head first.
- For protected one-on-one time and letting your child be the boss for a set stretch, the defiance guides lay out the how; both pay off here too.

## What To Say

- "You want the cookie now. I know. Ten seconds of waiting-practice first — count with me."
- "Give me your biggest, silliest NO. Ha! My turn."
- "Let's do a practice run of leaving the park — totally pretend, we'll be goofy about it."
- To yourself: "Kindest believable reason: he's wiped, not defiant."

## Common Pitfalls

- Only ever building these muscles mid-crisis — the one moment they aren't loaded yet.
- Reading "do less" as neglect. It's an active choice for safe, low-stakes resistance only, never for anything unsafe.
- Practicing waiting so long or so often it turns into a punishment instead of a game.
- Saving your generous read for after you've already snapped.

## When To Seek Support

If your child can't tolerate even the smallest wait without distress far beyond same-age peers, or resistance is constant across every setting despite steady connection, check in with your pediatrician. See the red-flags card.

articles.title: Getting Through the Hard Moment
articles.description: When cooperation has to happen right now, you need a path, not a louder voice.
articles.content:
# Getting Through the Hard Moment

When cooperation has to happen right now, you need a path, not a louder voice. Steady yourself going in. Clear the predictable snag before it appears. Make the ask something your child can see and step into — a picture to follow, a game you briefly join. And expect it to wobble — planning for the wobble is what keeps you from bailing at the first "no."

## Why This Works

Above a certain heat, no technique works, so the real job is keeping the moment under that line — and most of that happens before it starts. One small move ahead of a known friction point (the thing you always fight about) lowers the temperature before anyone's upset. Your own state is the next lever: kids catch your calm or your panic, and calm here just means a notch steadier than your gut reaction, not serene. Turning a spoken list into something your child can see — a row of little pictures, a countable set of steps — does two things at once: it sidesteps the working-memory overload from the last chapter, and it moves the "boss" of the moment off of you and onto the chart, so it's the two of you following it instead of you nagging them. A quick, true "this part's hard for me too" tells a child they're not uniquely bad at this — which changes how alone the moment feels, even if it doesn't make the task easier. And building the expectation of a wobble right into the plan means a stumble reads as normal, not as proof the whole thing failed.

## What To Do

- Steady yourself first with a short line of your own: "This part is loud. I can do loud." A notch calmer is the whole goal.
- Clear one thing in advance. Whatever the predictable snag is, remove or set it up before the moment — earlier, calmer, once.
- Show it, don't just say it: point along a simple picture-strip or count steps on your fingers, so there's something to follow that isn't your voice.
- Step briefly into their world before you end it: place one puzzle piece, admire the tower, THEN the ask. A shared line about hard stops rides along fine — "I hate closing my book mid-chapter too."
- Plan for the wobble. Decide now that it'll go sideways somewhere, and when it does, say a steadying line out loud and reconnect — don't push harder on the task.
- When a clock is genuinely against you, add one line just for you: late is a nuisance, not an emergency. The panic in your own body is what wrecks the other steps.
- For a snag that keeps recurring, talk it over together at a calm, unrelated time: "What makes leaving the park so hard? Let's solve it." That does more than any in-the-moment move.

## What To Say

- "Two more minutes, then we follow the picture-steps together."
- To yourself: "A notch calmer than my gut. That's enough."
- "Getting out the door is hard for me too. Okay — step one on the strip: shoes."
- "That went sideways — I rushed you. Let's breathe and find our spot again."

## Common Pitfalls

- Skipping the before and trying to fix a hot moment with words once it's already hot.
- Aiming for perfectly composed instead of one notch steadier — then giving up when you can't hit calm.
- Dumping the whole step-list at once instead of showing one step at a time.
- Treating the first wobble as proof it isn't working and abandoning the approach.

## When To Seek Support

If ordinary transitions routinely escalate into distress or aggression you can't keep safe, no matter how well you prepare, talk with your pediatrician. See the red-flags card.

articles.title: Meeting a Flat "No" Without a Standoff
articles.description: A single flat "no" is a fork in the road.
articles.content:
# Meeting a Flat "No" Without a Standoff

A single flat "no" is a fork in the road. Answer it with a bigger, louder ask and you get a standoff. Pause instead, name the wish underneath it, and let your child feel understood before you do anything else — and the "no" often loosens on its own. This is for a one-off refusal. A repeated pattern or a safety issue is the next chapter, where you act first.

## Why This Works

The instant you meet a refusal with a stronger counter-push, you stack resistance on resistance — now two people are dug in. A pause does the opposite: it opens a gap the child can sometimes close by themselves, no further input from you. When you do speak, aim under the "no" at what's driving it — a wish for more control, more time, more you — rather than at the literal word. Naming that wish ("you really wish this could wait") lands as being seen, and a child who feels seen has far less to push against. You don't have to understand or agree with the reason for this to work: honoring that the moment genuinely feels bad to them is its own move, and it comes before any shared sense of why. If a refusal hardens into a standoff anyway, mending the moment matters more than winning the original point — naming that something feels off between you comes first, ahead of re-asking. And sometimes a dose of silliness cuts the tension faster than any of it: the same connection, delivered through play.

## What To Do

- Pause before you answer a "no." Count to three. Let the gap do some of the work.
- Name the wish under the refusal instead of the refusal itself: more time, more say, more you.
- Validate the feeling without needing the reason — you can honor that this feels bad to them even when it makes no sense to you.
- If it hardens into a standoff, drop the original ask for a beat and mend the moment first. The point isn't worth the rupture.
- Reach for playfulness when tension spikes — a silly voice, a slow-motion bit — to break the deadlock through fun instead of force.
- Step back to signal trust: make the ask, then busy yourself nearby instead of standing over them, and give them room to come to it on their own.

## What To Say

- "Hmm. Okay, hang on." (Then actually pause.)
- "You really wish you could keep going. That makes sense — stopping's no fun."
- "You've got a reason, even if it isn't in words yet. I'm taking it seriously."
- "Hold on — I forgot my slowly-counting magic voice. Oooone… twooo…"

## Common Pitfalls

- Meeting the first "no" with a louder second ask — resistance stacked on resistance.
- Asking "why?" and expecting a clear answer, when the child couldn't name the reason if they tried.
- Making your validation conditional on the reason making sense to you.
- Chasing compliance so hard you blow past a rupture that now matters more than the task.

## When To Seek Support

If nearly every ordinary request turns into an entrenched standoff for weeks despite pausing and connecting, or refusals come with intense distress that won't settle, loop in your pediatrician. See the red-flags card.

articles.title: When Words Aren't Enough
articles.description: Some moments aren't solved by better talking.
articles.content:
# When Words Aren't Enough

Some moments aren't solved by better talking. If you've asked your child to stop the same thing five times, the missing piece usually isn't another reminder — it's you stepping in with your own body or the setup of the room. What makes something a real boundary, and how to redirect an urge instead of only blocking it, live in the defiance and discipline guides. This chapter is the listening-specific version: following through yourself, and handling the moments that turn unsafe.

## Why This Works

A child who keeps doing the thing after being told to stop usually can't stop on their own yet — and each repeated "stop" with no change from you quietly confirms that no one is actually going to help. What helps is you doing something, not repeating the words: moving the object, shifting your position, stepping between your child and the trouble. The wording matters too — trading a thin "please stop" for a plain statement of what you're about to do supplies the leadership the child couldn't summon alone. The deeper mechanics — the test of whether a limit even counts as a boundary (does it need your child's cooperation to work?) — are covered in the defiance guides, and giving a blocked urge somewhere to go rather than only walling it off is covered there and in the discipline guides; both apply straight to listening. What's specific here is the follow-through: the moment repeating stops working, you stop repeating and start doing.

## What To Do

- When you've said "stop" more than twice, change something on your side instead of saying it again: move the item, shift your body, take a hand.
- Swap thin please-stop language for what you'll do: not "we don't climb on that," but "I'm going to lift you down, and then we'll find something safe to climb."
- If a moment turns genuinely unsafe — heading for the road, something sharp, a hit about to land — act first and talk after. Secure the child or remove the hazard, then connect. Safety doesn't wait for a conversation.
- Keep choices for the how and the when, never for whether a safety limit holds. A non-negotiable stays non-negotiable.
- When a child who's learned "it's my body" turns those words against a needed care task, honor the words and keep the task moving — you can tell them their no is heard and still finish what has to happen, gently.
- When your child listens for one grown-up but not another, skip the blame and check two things: was the limit clear and specific, and is the everyday connection with that person as strong as it could be.

## What To Say

- "I've asked twice. Now I'm going to help." (Then do it, calmly.)
- "I'm moving this over here so it stops being a fight."
- "Stopping this is on me right now — I'll keep you safe while your body learns."
- "You don't want the sunscreen. I hear you. I'm still keeping your skin safe — quick and gentle."

## Common Pitfalls

- Repeating "stop" a tenth time when the ninth already failed — repetition isn't a boundary.
- Waiting until a safe-enough moment turns unsafe before you finally step in.
- Turning a genuine non-negotiable into a negotiation because your child pushed.
- Hearing "it's my body" and either overriding it coldly or dropping a truly necessary care task — you can respect the words and still keep them safe.

## When To Seek Support

If your child regularly can't be kept safe during ordinary non-compliance, or a needed care routine is impossible without force that distresses everyone, talk with your pediatrician. If a child's use of body-autonomy language ever points to something that frightens or confuses them, treat it seriously and seek professional guidance. See the red-flags card.

articles.title: In Public, and Coming Back Together After
articles.description: Two moments test every parent: when your child won't cooperate in front of an audience, and when you lose it and snap.
articles.content:
# In Public, and Coming Back Together After

Two moments test every parent: when your child won't cooperate in front of an audience, and when you lose it and snap. For the public one, the first move is calming yourself, not managing your child — an unspoken "everyone's judging me" is what tips you into too-harsh or too-soft. For the snap, what matters is the coming-back-together afterward, and the repairing guides cover how to do that in full.

## Why This Works

In public, what drives an over-harsh crackdown or a total cave-in usually isn't your child's behavior — it's the story running in your own head about what the onlookers think. Quiet that first, and you handle the moment about as evenly as you would at home. Since you can't actually know what a stranger is thinking, you're free to pick the kinder guess: it costs you nothing to imagine the parent watching is remembering their own hard days rather than grading yours. The harder-won skill is being firm and warm at the same time — a clear limit delivered with an open face, not a cold crackdown and not a mushy plea — which is exactly what an audience makes hardest, so it's worth rehearsing when no one's watching. As for snapping: raising your voice sometimes isn't proof you've failed or that any of this is broken. It's an ordinary part of imperfect parenting, and what your child carries depends far more on what you do next than on the moment itself. The repair itself — how to own it, name it, and come back — is the whole subject of the repairing guides. What's specific here is that the rupture happened over cooperation, so the repair names that.

## What To Do

- In public, steady yourself before you touch the situation: a quick private line like "I can handle this, and I don't owe the room a performance."
- Choose the generous guess about onlookers — most have stood exactly where you're standing — because the harsh guess is no likelier to be true and costs you far more.
- Aim for firm and warm together: the limit stays, your face stays kind. Rehearse the combination at home so it's there under the spotlight.
- After you snap, steady yourself first — one incident isn't a verdict on you — before you turn back to your child.
- Then reconnect over what happened, naming the cooperation piece: that you got loud about the shoes, that it wasn't their fault you yelled, and what you'll try next time. The repairing guides walk through this step by step.
- Let the repair count for more than the rupture — coming back rebuilds trust past where it started.

## What To Say

- To yourself, in public: "This is mine to handle. The audience isn't the point."
- "You're having a hard time leaving, and that's okay — we're still going. I'll help you."
- After a snap: "I yelled about the shoes. That was me losing my cool, not your fault. Let's start over."
- "I don't like how I sounded just now. Can we have a do-over?"

## Common Pitfalls

- Letting the imagined audience push you into a harsher or softer response than you'd ever choose in private.
- Going cold-firm or mushy-soft, when the moment needs firmness and warmth at once.
- Rushing to repair while still flooded — steady your own head first.
- Treating a snap as proof the whole approach is broken, instead of an ordinary moment with a repair after it.

## When To Seek Support

If snapping is tipping into frequent yelling you can't rein in, or public moments leave you raging or panicked, that's your own nervous system asking for support — reach out. See the red-flags card, and the repairing guides for the repair itself.

scripts.title: Dinner's Ready and They Haven't Budged
scripts.scenario: Dinner is on the table going cold. Your child is on the living-room floor, deep in a long parade of toy animals, and hasn't moved after three calls of "come eat."

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
Go to them, get low, join for ten seconds first: "Whoa — look at this parade. Who's the leader?"

Then the ask, with a nearer reason: "The animals can guard the table while we eat — food's hot now, and you get to pick your seat."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Cross the room instead of calling across it — a request needs connection to travel on
- Name what they're doing before you name what you need
- Give one small choice or nearer reason, not a lecture about cold food
- Keep it to a single step: come to the table now; everything else waits

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: If calling from the kitchen keeps failing, make "I come to you first" the default, and build a two-minute heads-up into the run-up to meals.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: Prioritize safety. Avoid physical restraint unless needed to prevent imminent harm. Follow local guidance; seek professional support if unsure.

scripts.title: A Flat "No" to Putting It Away
scripts.scenario: You ask, calm and just once, for the crayons to be capped and the coloring cleared before lunch. Your child doesn't move — just a flat "No."

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
Pause first: "Hmm. Okay." (Actually stop for three seconds.)

Name the wish under the no: "You're not done. You wish coloring could just keep going."

Validate without needing the reason: "Stopping feels wrong to you somehow. Okay — I don't need the why to take it seriously."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Don't answer the first "no" with a bigger second ask — that stacks resistance
- Aim under the refusal at the wish driving it, not the word itself
- Offer a bridge, not a battle: "One last color, then we clear it together"
- If tension spikes, break it with silliness before you break it with force

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: If it hardens into a standoff, mend the moment before re-asking. A predictable "last-color" ritual makes the stop easier next time.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: Prioritize safety. Avoid physical restraint unless needed to prevent imminent harm. Follow local guidance; seek professional support if unsure.

scripts.title: Bedtime Takes an Hour, One Stall at a Time
scripts.scenario: Bedtime is a marathon. Every step — bath, pajamas, teeth — turns into its own negotiation, and a twenty-minute routine sprawls into an hour.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
Step into their world for a beat — one puzzle piece, one admiring look — before the ask. Let's do it together, just us and the picture-steps."

To yourself, going in: "Slow is normal here. A notch calmer than my gut."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Turn the routine into a visible strip of little pictures they can follow, so the chart leads instead of your voice
- Show and do one step at a time; don't announce the whole list at once
- Make it a gentle race or game rather than a series of orders
- Steady yourself first — your calm is doing half the work

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: At a calm, unrelated time, ask together what makes bedtime so hard and problem-solve it. Keep the picture-strip where the routine starts.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: Prioritize safety. Avoid physical restraint unless needed to prevent imminent harm. Follow local guidance; seek professional support if unsure.

scripts.title: Told to Stop Climbing, Right Back Up
scripts.scenario: Your child keeps climbing onto the back of the couch to leap off. You've said "get down" over and over, and each time they are right back up within a minute.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content: Stop repeating; state what you'll do: "I've asked a bunch of times, and that climb isn't safe — so I'm going to help you down now. Then let's find you a real climbing spot."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- When "stop" hasn't worked twice, act instead of saying it a third time — lift them down, calmly
- Change the setup: move a pile of floor cushions over as a spot that IS for jumping
- Give the climbing urge a home rather than only walling it off
- Keep your tone flat and warm; the action is the boundary, not the words

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: The defiance guides cover what makes this a real boundary (one that doesn't depend on your child agreeing); the discipline guides cover redirecting the urge. Both apply straight to this moment.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: Prioritize safety. Supervise climbing and secure furniture that can tip. Avoid physical restraint beyond gently moving your child to safety. Follow local guidance; seek professional support if unsure.

scripts.title: "Just a Minute" During Your Work Block
scripts.scenario: You have thirty minutes of work to finish at the kitchen table. Your child keeps drifting over every couple of minutes — a question, a snack request, a thing to show you.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content: Connect and set it up in advance: "I have grown-up work for two timer-turns. Here's your own work box, right next to me. When the timer sings, I'm all yours for a giant hug."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Make a deposit of real attention first, before the work block, not only after
- Set up a parallel activity within sight so they're near you, not shut out
- Use a visible timer so the wait has a shape they can see
- Name the reunion clearly, then keep that promise the second it sings

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: Start with short blocks and stretch them as it works. Topping up connection before the block prevents most of the interruptions during it.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: Prioritize safety. Avoid physical restraint unless needed to prevent imminent harm. Follow local guidance; seek professional support if unsure.

scripts.title: The Silent Wall When the Screen Ends
scripts.scenario: The tablet show is ending and your child goes silent — not a "no," just a wall. Every reminder slides off. They don't move, don't argue, don't stop.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
Set the ending before it starts: "Two shows left, then the tablet goes to sleep — you get to start the timer."

At the handover, playful: "Uh oh… the tablet's yawning. It's SO sleepy. Say night-night."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Decide and announce the ending up front — the fight is almost always the ending, not the middle
- Let them start the timer, so some control is theirs
- Bring humor to the switch-off instead of a countdown of warnings
- Treat the silent wall as overwhelm, not defiance — make the "off" a step you do together

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: At a calm time, decide the screen-ending routine together. A wall that repeats is a sign the ending needs a plan, not more reminders.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: Prioritize safety. Avoid physical restraint unless needed to prevent imminent harm. Follow local guidance; seek professional support if unsure.

scripts.title: Everything Has to Be Now
scripts.scenario: The instant your child wants something — a snack, a turn, your attention — it has to be NOW, and even "one minute" tips them straight into a meltdown.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content: Name it as practice and validate the hard part: "You want it right now, and waiting feels awful. Let's grow the waiting muscle — count to five with me, then it's yours."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Build small, deliberate waits at calm, low-stakes times, not only when a real wait is forced on them
- Narrate and validate the wait every time — "waiting's hard" — so it never feels like a punishment
- Start tiny (a count of three) and stretch it as tolerance grows
- Follow through the moment the wait is done, so the practice stays trustworthy

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: The muscle has to be built before it's needed. A child who has practiced waiting at snack time has something to draw on when the wait is real.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: Prioritize safety. Avoid physical restraint unless needed to prevent imminent harm. Follow local guidance; seek professional support if unsure.

scripts.title: Listens for One of You, Not the Other
scripts.scenario: Your child cooperates smoothly for one caregiver and pushes back on nearly everything with the other — and the less-listened-to grown-up is starting to feel like the bad guy.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content: Between the adults, no blame: "It isn't you, and it isn't favoritism. Let's check two boring things — are my limits as clear and specific as yours, and does our just-us time need a top-up?"

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Skip the blame entirely — this is two fixable variables, not a ranking of parents
- Check limit clarity: vague timing ("in a bit") lands as an unclear boundary; specific and concrete lands better
- Check the everyday connection with the less-listened-to caregiver, and build it deliberately
- Adjust both together rather than one person trying harder in the moment

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: Usually it's clarity plus connection, not love or favoritism. Re-check after a couple of weeks of clearer limits and more one-on-one time.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: Prioritize safety. Avoid physical restraint unless needed to prevent imminent harm. Follow local guidance; seek professional support if unsure.

scripts.title: "It's My Body" Aimed at Sunscreen
scripts.scenario: You've taught your child that their body is theirs and they can always say stop — good and important — and now they are using those exact words to refuse sunscreen before the pool.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content: Honor the words and keep the task: "You're right — your body is yours, and you can always tell me stop. Sunscreen isn't a choice, because it keeps your skin from getting hurt. I'm going to help, quick and gentle. You pick: arms first or legs first?"

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Genuinely honor the consent words — don't override them coldly or pretend they weren't said
- Keep the necessary care happening; a health-and-safety task isn't up for negotiation
- Offer a real choice over how or in what order, never over whether
- Stay warm and quick; the goal is done and gentle, not a debate

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: Keep teaching the "my body" language for genuinely optional touch. A calmly-named exception for necessary care doesn't undo it.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: This applies to non-negotiable health and safety care only. If a child's use of body-autonomy language ever points to something that frightens or confuses them, treat it seriously and seek professional guidance. Avoid physical restraint beyond the minimum gentle help needed.

scripts.title: Five Minutes to Leave, Zero Cooperation
scripts.scenario: You have to be out the door in five minutes for a pickup you can't be late for, and your child is flat-out resisting boots and coat.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
To yourself first: "Late is a nuisance, not an emergency. My panic is the real problem here."

To your child, firm and warm, one step: "We're leaving in five, and I'll help your body get there. Boots first — do you want the fast way or the silly way into them?"

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Steady your own manufactured-emergency feeling before anything else; it's what wrecks your patience
- Keep it to one step at a time, not the whole leaving sequence
- Be firm and warm together — the limit holds, your tone stays kind
- If the clock truly demands it, help them into things calmly rather than winning an argument

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: If leaving on time is a recurring battle, plan the departure routine together at a calm moment — that fixes more than any rushed morning ever will.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: Prioritize safety. Avoid physical restraint unless needed to prevent imminent harm. Follow local guidance; seek professional support if unsure.

scripts.title: The Meltdown With an Audience
scripts.scenario: At the library, your child flops down and refuses to leave when it's time — and now a couple of other parents are watching to see how you'll handle it.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
To yourself first: "I've got this. The room isn't the point, and I don't owe it a performance."

To your child, warm and clear: "Hard to leave when it's cozy here. We're still going — you can walk with me, or I can carry you. You choose."

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Calm your own audience-panic before you touch the situation; that panic is what tips you too-harsh or too-soft
- Assume the watchers remember their own hard days — it's no less likely than judgment, and far kinder to you
- Stay firm and warm at once; offer a choice over how you leave, not whether
- Handle it the way you would at home, because the audience changes you, not the child

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: Rehearse the firm-and-warm combination at home, where it's easy. Under the spotlight it's harder to improvise, so having it ready helps.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: Prioritize safety. Avoid physical restraint unless needed to prevent imminent harm. Follow local guidance; seek professional support if unsure.

scripts.title: You Yelled About the Shoes
scripts.scenario: You asked five times to get shoes on, then you yelled — loud enough that your child went quiet and teary. Now you want to come back from it.

steps.title: What to say
steps.content:
To yourself first: "One loud moment isn't the whole story. I can come back from this."

To your child, once you're steady: "I yelled about the shoes. That was too big, and it wasn't your fault. I'm going to work on my volume. Want a do-over hug?"

steps.title: What to do
steps.content:
- Settle your own nervous system before you approach — repair while still flooded rarely lands
- Keep it short and specific: name the cooperation moment you got loud about
- Take your part without piling any fault onto your child
- Let the repair count for more than the rupture; coming back builds trust past where it started

steps.title: Follow-up
steps.content: The repairing guides walk through the full how of a repair conversation. What's specific here is naming that it happened over listening — so the repair names that too.

steps.title: Safety note
steps.content: Prioritize safety. Avoid physical restraint unless needed to prevent imminent harm. Follow local guidance; seek professional support if unsure.
